extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century coffee-house/public readers interested in social satire and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical essays and social satire describing clubs, manners, and the art of beauty (conduct, membership rules, and moral guidance) as presented to an early-18th-century public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amorous Club admission requirement: mistress plus poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate: Without the latter no one can be admitted; for he that is not in love enough to rhime, is unqualified for our Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission is secret due to University constraints; membership also governed by statutes (oral/recorded 'in our own Breasts'); presidency bestowed by dignity of passion; examples: poem + mistress are the explicit entrance conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amorous Club rule: prohibition on speaking disrespectfully of any woman
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak disrespectfully of any Woman, is Expulsion from our gentle Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an absolute rule of membership—disrespect leads to expulsion. The club enforces a civility-based standard regarding members' speech about women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amorous Club behavioural norms: performative self-addressing and tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are not obliged to make any Introduction to his Discourse, but at once ... speaks in the Thread of his own Thoughts ... in this Assembly they do not meet to talk to each other, but every Man claims the full Liberty of talking to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of snuff-boxes and canes, members handle tokens (ribbon, broken fan, old girdle) while they talk of the fair person remembered by each respective token; rhetorical devices include sighing, gestures, dumb-show; one may rise to make a passionate discourse that the whole company joins in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amorous Club conversational etiquette: avoid direct answers and perform prescribed affect
rubrics_metrics.description: We look upon a Man as no Company, that does not sigh five times in a Quarter of an Hour; and look upon a Member as very absurd, that is so much himself as to make a direct Answer to a Question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are expected to display signs of transported passion (sighing, rhetorical evasiveness) rather than straightforward replies; affectation of loverly melancholy is a membership norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidency awarded by degree of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Presidentship is bestow'd according to the Dignity of Passion; ... if any Man has declared the Violence of his Flame in more pathetick Terms, he is made President for that Night, out of respect to his superior Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership within the club is meritocratic by theatrical display of passion rather than by conventional office, encouraging performative competition in expression of love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative example: dress-only expressions of passion are shallow (Fringe-Glove Club critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: These Fellows could express their Passion in nothing but their Dress; but the Oxonians are Fantastical now they are Lovers, in proportion to their Learning and Understanding before they became such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique functions as a normative standard: true (interesting) passion should produce varied follies and inventive behaviour, not mere fashionable dress; clubs that limit expression to attire lack variety and soon 'dropp'd.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Project originality standard (implicit critique of the 'Projector')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Projector's design of an opera draws on and recombines many existing stage diversions; his plan is presented as a humorous example of a scheme lacking proper originality or practical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The satirical treatment implies evaluative criteria for entertainments: originality, coherence, appropriateness of spectacle to subject (e.g., puppet-shows and dancing monkeys for Alexander the Great are ludicrous), and practical feasibility (performers, language). Examples/anti-patterns: borrowing disparate spectacles from other pieces and inserting unsuitable entertainments (Bull-baiting excluded only for physical roof constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary maxim 1: no woman is handsome by force of features alone
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman can be Handsome by the Force of Features alone, any more than she can be Witty only by the Help of Speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical features alone do not constitute true handsomeness; other qualities and accomplishments are required. This is presented as a foundational principle before giving instruction on 'improving Beauty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary maxim 2: pride and affectation undermine beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: That Pride destroys all Symmetry and Grace, and Affectation is a more terrible Enemy to fine Faces than the Small-Pox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity and artificial behaviour are described as active deformities: they cancel natural grace; advice implies cultivating modesty and genuine comportment rather than ostentation or mannered poses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary maxim 3: (verbatim) relation of beauty and falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman is capable of being Beautiful, who is not incapable of being False.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paradoxical-sounding maxim is stated as a preliminary principle; surrounding text uses it to argue that sincere virtues (truthfulness, good humour, innocence) animate beauty—falsehood and coquetry spoil it. The original phrasing is retained because the essay treats it as an axiom to be unpacked rather than as a clear single-clause rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary maxim 4: vices acceptable in friends are intolerable in lovers
rubrics_metrics.description: And, That what would be Odious in a Friend, is Deformity in a Mistress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavior that may be forgivable or tolerated in ordinary friendships becomes disqualifying when one is an object of desire; social context raises standards for conduct when someone is a romantic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art of assisting beauty: cultivate virtues and accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities. By this Help alone it is that those who are the Favourite Work of Nature ... become animated, and are in a Capacity of exerting their Charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance emphasizes moral and intellectual qualities (innocence, piety, good humour, truth) over cosmetics; examples: Miltons' Adam describing Eve by 'Lustre of her Mind'; Ben Johnson epitaph quoted to illustrate that virtue gives vigour to beauty. Anti-patterns: reliance on cosmetics or superficial 'false helps' sold by quacks; cosmetics entertain the eye but do not affect the heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-consequence principle: flattering attention vs. acquired accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Consciousness of her Charms has rendered her insupportably Vain ... Daphne ... was obliged to acquire some Accomplishments to make up for the want of those Attractions which she saw in her Sister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative-observational standard: praise without corrective demands breeds vanity and bad companionship skills, whereas lack of outward attraction can motivate genuine accomplishments—thus cultivation of sense and accomplishments is a better route to agreeable company than mere beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ugly-Club philosophical standard: value what lies beyond mere appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing ought to be laudable in a Man, in which his Will is not concerned; therefore our Society can follow Nature, and where she has thought fit, as it were, to mock herself, we can do so too, and be merry upon the Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle justifies the Ugly-Club's contempt of beauty: laud what the agent consciously chooses; mock natural, involuntary attributes. It functions as a normative stance about what merits praise and what social satire may target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit's license: authorship and masks as permissible disguises
rubrics_metrics.description: That Wits were privileged to wear what Masks they pleased in all Ages; and that a Vizard had been the constant Crown of their Labours ... 'Larvati' or 'Larvâ donati' of the Ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim serves as a normative justification for satirists and wits using persona, mask, and liberty in speech and writing; examples cited include classical frontispieces and literary precedent, bounding what is allowable in satirical/critical discourse.
